title: The food matrix question
intro: A food is more than its nutrient list. Nutrients come packed in a structure (the food 'matrix') of cells, fibre, fats, proteins and thousands of other compounds, and that package changes how they are digested and what they do. Animal and plant foods both have one, and the claims below test what research says about each.

claims.claim: Animal foods deliver nutrients in a complete, highly digestible package (the 'animal matrix')
claims.summary: Part of this holds up. Meat, fish, eggs and dairy contain all the essential amino acids (the protein building blocks the body can't make) in proportions close to what the body uses, and their protein is digested well. They also carry iron partly as haem iron and vitamin A as retinol, forms the body takes up easily (see the absorption section). In short laboratory studies, higher-quality proteins, mostly animal ones, raised muscle protein building slightly more than lower-quality ones; a 2021 review of 27 studies called the effect small. The whole food seems to add something: in a trial with 10 young men, whole eggs stimulated muscle protein building after exercise more than egg whites with the same protein. But in longer training studies the gap largely closes when people eat enough protein: a review of 9 trials found soy and animal proteins gave similar gains in muscle and strength, and in a 12-week study habitual vegans and meat eaters on the same protein intake (about 1.6 g per kg of body weight a day, partly from powders) gained the same. Most of this research tested protein powders rather than whole meals, so it says little about the matrix as a whole.
whyThisGrade: Differences in protein quality are measured directly and are consistent
The advantage in short muscle-building studies is small and mostly disappears in longer trials when protein intake is adequate
Most trials used isolated protein powders, not whole foods; the whole-egg trial had only 10 participants
Long-term health outcomes of whole animal versus whole plant foods are rarely compared directly

claims.claim: Cheese doesn't raise cholesterol as much as its saturated fat would predict (the 'dairy matrix')
claims.summary: Compared with butter, yes. A pooled analysis of 5 randomised trials found hard cheese lowered LDL cholesterol (low-density lipoprotein, the 'bad' kind) by about 6.5 % compared with butter with a similar fat profile, and lowered HDL ('good') cholesterol a little too. In a 6-week trial with 164 adults, the same amount of dairy fat raised total and LDL cholesterol less when it was eaten as full-fat cheese than as butter with added casein and calcium. So the cheese package changes how its fat acts. But the effect is relative to butter: in the same trials, cheese raised LDL compared with tofu or fat-modified cheese, as its fat profile predicts. For heart disease itself, the evidence is observational: in 29 cohort studies with about 940,000 people, total dairy and milk were neutral, and a small 2 % lower risk of heart and blood vessel disease per 10 g of cheese a day weakened when one large Swedish study was removed. An expert workshop concluded that dairy's effects can't be judged from its nutrient content alone, and that more research is needed.
whyThisGrade: Randomised trials, but few and small (5 trials in the cheese-versus-butter analysis)
Mostly compared with butter; against plant foods and unsaturated fats cheese still raised LDL
Heart outcome data are observational, and the small cheese association was not robust
Why it happens (calcium, protein, the structure of the fat, fermentation) is not settled

claims.claim: Fibre from whole plant foods protects against heart disease, diabetes and bowel cancer
claims.summary: Fibre comes only from plant foods; meat, fish, eggs and dairy contain none. A large set of reviews, partly funded by the World Health Organization (WHO), covering 185 cohort studies covering about 135 million person-years, and 58 trials with 4,635 adults, found that people eating the most fibre had 15–30 % lower rates of death from all causes and from heart disease, and of coronary heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes and bowel (colorectal) cancer, than those eating the least. In the trials, more fibre lowered body weight, blood pressure and total cholesterol. The lowest risks were seen at about 25–29 g a day, and the certainty of the evidence for fibre was rated moderate. An earlier review of 25 cohort studies found 10 % lower bowel cancer risk per 10 g of fibre a day, mainly from cereal fibre and whole grains. These reviews looked at fibre in food and left out supplements, and the disease results come from observational studies, where people eating more fibre also differ in other ways.
whyThisGrade: Many large cohort studies agree, with a clear dose-response
Randomised trials confirm effects on risk factors (weight, blood pressure, cholesterol), though not on disease itself
Disease outcomes come from observational data, which can be confounded by other healthy habits
The reviews themselves rated the certainty for fibre as moderate

claims.claim: Fibre is unnecessary, and cutting it out fixes gut problems
claims.summary: Fibre isn't an essential nutrient in the way vitamin C is, and some people do feel better with less of certain kinds. The main study behind the 'zero fibre' idea followed 63 people with long-standing constipation who were told to stop or cut fibre; those who did reported fewer symptoms. But it had no comparison group chosen at random, people chose their own diet, and it was small. Randomised trials point the other way for most people: in 14 trials with 906 people with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), fibre supplements helped (about 1 in 10 people treated improved because of it), but only soluble fibre such as psyllium; wheat bran showed no clear benefit. EFSA (the European Food Safety Authority) set an adequate intake of 25 g a day for adults, based on normal bowel function. Fibre-rich foods can also lower the uptake of some minerals, partly through phytate (see the absorption section). Against this, the large body of evidence linking fibre-rich diets with lower rates of heart disease, diabetes and bowel cancer has no counterpart showing harm from fibre at usual intakes.
whyThisGrade: The main study supporting the claim was small, uncontrolled and not randomised
Randomised trials in IBS are short and test supplements, not whole-food diets
Responses differ by type of fibre and by person
No long-term studies show health benefits from very low-fibre diets

claims.claim: Eating more fruit and vegetables lowers the risk of heart disease and early death
claims.summary: In a review of 95 cohort studies, each extra 200 g of fruit and vegetables a day went with 8 % lower risk of coronary heart disease, 16 % lower risk of stroke, 3 % lower risk of cancer and 10 % lower risk of death from any cause. Risk kept falling up to about 800 g a day (600 g for cancer). Apples and pears, citrus, green leafy and cruciferous vegetables (cabbage family) stood out. The form of the food seems to matter: in three US cohorts with about 187,000 people, whole fruits such as blueberries, grapes and apples were linked with lower risk of type 2 diabetes, while fruit juice was linked with higher risk (8 % per 3 glasses a week). All of this is observational. People who eat more fruit and vegetables also tend to smoke less, move more and be better off, and studies can only partly adjust for that. There are no large trials of eating more fruit and vegetables with deaths as the outcome.
whyThisGrade: Observational studies only; healthier people may simply eat more fruit and vegetables
Results are consistent across many cohorts and show a dose-response, which adds some confidence
Intake is measured with food questionnaires, which are imprecise
No long randomised trials with hard outcomes such as deaths

claims.claim: A nutrient does the same thing in a pill as in the food it comes from
claims.summary: Beta-carotene is the classic warning case. In cohort studies, people with more carotenoids in their diet or blood had about 21 % lower lung cancer risk, though the authors note this may just mark a diet rich in fruit and vegetables or leftover effects of smoking. When beta-carotene was tested as a pill, it did not prevent lung cancer, and in two large trials, ATBC (29,133 male smokers) and CARET (18,314 smokers and asbestos workers), it increased it. A review of 9 trials found 20–30 mg a day raised lung cancer by 16 % and stomach cancer too, in smokers and asbestos workers. More broadly, 78 trials of antioxidant pills (beta-carotene, vitamins A, C and E, selenium) with about 297,000 people found no fall in deaths; in the better-run trials, beta-carotene and vitamin E slightly raised it. Pill doses were far above food amounts, so these trials don't show that food beta-carotene is harmful, only that a food's effect can't be predicted from one isolated ingredient.
whyThisGrade: Large randomised trials with hard outcomes for the supplements
The food side is observational and may reflect a healthier lifestyle
Supplement doses were much higher than food provides, so trials and cohorts test different exposures
Shown clearly for beta-carotene and a few antioxidants; it can't be assumed for every nutrient

claims.claim: A food's nutrient list tells you everything it does in the body
claims.summary: Food composition tables track about 150 nutrients, while more than 26,000 distinct compounds are known to occur in food, most of them (such as many polyphenols) never measured in a typical table. This is sometimes called nutritional dark matter, and it applies to animal and plant foods alike. Structure matters as well as content. In almonds, chewing breaks open only the outer layer of cells, and intact cells with their fat still inside show up in stool. In a controlled feeding trial with 18 adults, almonds provided about 4.6 kcal per gram, 32 % less than the 6.0–6.1 kcal per gram their nutrient list predicts. Cheese and butter with similar fats act differently on cholesterol (see the dairy claim). What most of the unmeasured compounds do in the body is simply unknown, which is one reason measuring your own markers before and after a change can tell you more than a table.
whyThisGrade: The gap between known and tracked compounds is documented directly
Matrix effects such as the almond findings come from controlled measurements, though in small studies
How much the unmeasured compounds matter for health is largely unknown

claims.claim: Red and processed meat cause bowel cancer
claims.summary: In 2015 the World Health Organization's cancer agency, IARC (International Agency for Research on Cancer), reviewed more than 800 studies and classed processed meat (ham, bacon, sausages and other cured or smoked meat) as a cause of bowel (colorectal) cancer, and unprocessed red meat as a probable cause. That classification says how sure they are that it can cause cancer, not how large the risk is. A review of cohort studies found 18 % higher risk per 50 g of processed meat a day and 17 % per 100 g of red meat a day. In absolute terms that is a small change for one person, because bowel cancer starts from a fairly low lifetime risk. In 2019 the NutriRECS reviews of the same kind of evidence (cohorts with more than 6 million people) rated it low or very low certainty and the absolute effects of eating 3 fewer servings a week as very small, and their panel did not advise people to change how much meat they eat (a weak recommendation). Both sides agree the evidence is observational and stronger for processed than unprocessed meat; they differ on how much weight small risks from such studies deserve.
whyThisGrade: Only observational studies, with possible confounding and imprecise food questionnaires
Associations are consistent across many cohorts and show a dose-response
Relative increases are moderate; absolute differences per person are small
Expert groups reading the same evidence reached different conclusions
